turn_text: I think one cool thing that you've been working on this year and you've worked on for the past few years with Assemblymember Lowe is getting 17-year-olds, I guess, the right to vote in the primary election before they turn 18. Can you talk to us about that achievement? I know that's something that your father had worked on prior and how you think that's going to look on the November ballot.

Yeah, this was very fortuitous set of circumstances this year for us to finally get that across the finish line. My father initiated that effort. It really started when he was the government teacher at South San Francisco High School. He would often Yet his kids involved in local city council meetings and school board meetings, and I think he would give them extra credit if they got involved in any particular city council campaign. He never steered them in one direction or the other and never steered them certainly from a partisan standpoint. But he really wanted to encourage young people to get involved in civic affairs and in local government in particular. Local government is where he really believes that young people could have a direct impact and they could see the impact of their efforts. So that started him thinking about what are some other ways to get young people engaged early in voting and in politics and maybe that kind of fires their interests and aspirations themselves. So he took that classroom experience when he came to the Capitol and introduced the ACA a number of times. He did it at least twice. Some of his colleagues stepped up and sort of carried that. baton forward and then I've tried it myself a couple of different times so we finally this year we're able to garner the two-thirds vote in both the assembly and the senate to put it on the ballot and what's sort of interesting it's actually a little surprising that it's been so hard for that to happen because it's already in place in 18 other states so-called red states and blue states. Some of the most Republican states in the country allow 17-year-olds to vote in the primary. But unfortunately, it got framed in a partisan context for some reason in California. And it's just not a partisan issue. Young people are actually trending toward no-party preference, as a matter of fact. So it's not as though this will be some kind of a boom to the Democratic Party. And I did get bipartisan support. And we were able to get this on the ballot. And the key though I should mention I need to give a shout out to my colleague Evan Lowe, who had his own version of this, which is a straight lowering of the voting age across the board to 17. His effort got held up. He sort of rolled in with my effort. And we've been able to double team now, proposition 18. And that's going to be on the ballot. It's a little interesting numbering of proposition 18 with the 17 year old primary vote. But we're actually using that as an opportunity to remind people that these young people still have to be 18 by the general election. This would just enable them to participate in the primary. Sort of looking at the election as a full-cycle primary and general, which is the way we should be viewing it. But it sort of builds on the pre-registration program that Secretary of State Alex Padilla has put in place, a very successful program. I think close to 200,000 young people have pre-registered. So it's sort of building on those efforts to engage our young people. I'm hoping that it's going to be successful in November, but one, frankly, never really knows how the public is going to view this. I don't have access to any polling or anything like that. I just think it's a modest, reasonable expansion of voting rights for young people, and I'm certainly hoping that it will be successful, and I will be very much involved in the campaign this fall.

So I'm part of this working group. It's led by Phil Tang in the assembly, our budget chair, Senator Hertzberg, the majority leader in the Senate. Those two leaders have taken charge of this. My involvement came because I was one of the joint authors of a climate resiliency and jobs and infrastructure bond, a $7 billion package coming out of the assembly, which really at the beginning of the year was very much climate resiliency focused. As the year unfolded, we thought to ourselves, look, we're going to need to steer this more in a job creating direction and really looking at our natural resources infrastructure across the state of California. What can we do to make investments in green jobs? How can we position ourselves maybe to take advantage of federal dollars that come with regard to climate and green jobs. So that efforts sort of lost momentum because of everything that was going on economically. I think there was maybe some reticence to go to the ballot. with all of the economic fallout that was happening, go to the ballot with a big fiscal measure. So we started looking at different alternatives, and I had a conversation with Senator Hertzberg. There's a way to move money quickly out onto the street, so to speak, to create jobs. But with a bond, you have to actually get the voter approval, of course. But it takes time to sell those bonds and to get the proceeds and invest those funds into jobs and projects, even if they're so-called shovel ready projects. It takes a while, whereas there are some other mechanisms with securitizing special funds, doing some borrowing against expected revenues from the federal government. There are some creative things that could be done in the short run. Candidly, I think much of this was designed to engage the governor on economic recovery, putting a framework out there for discussion, bicameral, hopefully bipartisan, and really try to engage this governor around economic recovery. He has this business and jobs task force headed by Tom Steyer, who is very much a leader on climate issues and green jobs issues. So we've had a number of conversations with him as well. So I'm hoping that some of these legislative efforts can blend with the administration's approaches on economic recovery working with that task force. The governor was pretty clear he didn't want that task force to just produce a report that sits on a shelf. There's a lot of good minds at that table and hopefully they engage with the legislature and the governor and we put a package together that really gets money out on the street At this moment, we have no idea, frankly, where the federal government is going to land. So it remains to be seen what actually comes together, but I have no doubt this is going to be a conversation into 2021 and probably 2022.
